clues.clue: This command copies an existing remote Git repository — including all its history and branches — to your local machine.
clues.explain: git clone downloads the full repository history and all branches from a remote URL, creating a local working copy linked to the original remote as 'origin'.

clues.clue: This command moves specific files from the working directory into the staging area, marking them to be included in the next commit.
clues.explain: git add moves changes into the staging area (index); only staged changes are included in the next commit, giving you precise control over what is recorded.

clues.clue: This command shows the differences between the staging area and the most recent commit, revealing what would be captured if you committed right now.
clues.response: What is git diff --staged (or git diff --cached)?
clues.explain: git diff --staged compares the index to HEAD, showing exactly which staged changes will be recorded in the next commit — the counterpart to plain git diff.

clues.clue: This branching model uses long-lived parallel release branches (e.g. develop, release, hotfix) governed by strict merge rules for managing complex, versioned software.
clues.explain: Git Flow defines long-lived branches (main, develop, release, hotfix, feature) with explicit merge rules — optimized for software with discrete release cycles, unlike trunk-based development.

clues.clue: In Git's object model, this object type stores a directory snapshot — mapping file names to blob SHA-1 hashes — and is referenced by every commit.
clues.explain: A tree object records a snapshot of a directory: each entry maps a filename to a blob (file content) or another tree (subdirectory), forming the file-system hierarchy Git stores per commit.

clues.clue: This Dockerfile instruction sets the base image for all subsequent build steps, and is required to appear as the first directive in every Dockerfile.
clues.explain: FROM declares the parent image (e.g. FROM ubuntu:22.04) and must be the first instruction in a Dockerfile; every subsequent RUN, COPY, and CMD builds on top of it.

clues.clue: This Docker CLI command lists all currently running containers, showing their container ID, image, status, and published port mappings.
clues.explain: docker ps lists running containers; add -a to include stopped ones. The PORTS column shows host-to-container port mappings configured at run time with -p.

clues.clue: In a multi-stage Dockerfile, this instruction copies a file or directory from a previous named build stage into the current stage, without carrying over that stage's tools.
clues.explain: COPY --from=<stage> lets you pull only the compiled artifact out of a heavy builder stage into a lean runtime image, which is the core mechanism of a multi-stage build.

clues.clue: This Linux kernel feature works alongside namespaces to enforce resource limits on containers, capping CPU, memory, and I/O for each container group.
clues.explain: Control groups (cgroups) limit and account for resource consumption — CPU, RAM, disk I/O — per container; together with namespaces they form the kernel foundation of container isolation.

clues.clue: This Docker storage driver implements the overlay filesystem by merging a lower read-only image-layer stack with an upper writable container layer, and is shown in `docker info`.
clues.response: What is the overlay2 storage driver?
clues.explain: overlay2 has long been the standard Linux storage driver, stacking read-only image layers under one writable layer via the kernel's OverlayFS. (Docker 29+ defaults to the containerd snapshotter, but overlay2 remains widely used.)

clues.clue: This Kubernetes object ensures that a copy of a specified Pod is always running on every eligible node in the cluster, used for agents such as log collectors.
clues.explain: A DaemonSet schedules exactly one copy of a Pod on every (or a selected subset of) node(s), making it ideal for cluster-wide daemons like log shippers and monitoring agents.

clues.clue: This Kubernetes Service type exposes a workload outside the cluster by provisioning a cloud provider load balancer with a public IP address.
clues.explain: A Service of type LoadBalancer instructs the cloud provider to create an external load balancer (with a public IP) that forwards traffic to the matching Pods, enabling external access.

clues.clue: This lower-level Kubernetes controller, created and managed by a Deployment, maintains a stable set of replica Pods running at any given time.
clues.explain: A ReplicaSet ensures a specified number of Pod replicas are always running; Deployments manage ReplicaSets automatically to orchestrate rolling updates and rollbacks.

clues.clue: This control plane component is the authoritative key-value store for all cluster state, and every other control plane component reads and writes through it.
clues.explain: etcd is the distributed key-value store that backs all Kubernetes cluster state; the API server is the only component that reads and writes etcd directly, and its availability is critical for the control plane.

clues.clue: This type of admission webhook validates an API request against policy rules and can reject the request outright — but unlike its mutating counterpart, it cannot modify the object.
clues.explain: A ValidatingAdmissionWebhook inspects the final (possibly already-mutated) object and either allows or denies the request; it cannot alter the object, unlike a MutatingAdmissionWebhook.

clues.clue: This extension of CI automatically deploys every change that passes the pipeline to a staging or production environment without a manual approval gate.
clues.explain: Continuous Deployment extends Continuous Integration by automatically releasing every passing build to production, removing the manual promotion step and requiring high test confidence.

clues.clue: This dedicated server or service stores versioned build artifacts and Docker images, acting as the single source of truth packages are promoted from during a pipeline.
clues.response: What is an artifact repository (or package registry)?
clues.explain: An artifact repository (e.g. Nexus, Artifactory, a container registry) stores versioned, immutable build outputs; pipelines push artifacts here after build and pull them for deployment stages.

clues.clue: This deployment strategy releases a new version alongside the old by sending a gradually increasing slice of real traffic to it, using weighted routing rules in the load balancer.
clues.response: What is a canary deployment (or canary release)?
clues.explain: A canary deployment shifts traffic incrementally to the new version — e.g. 5%, then 25%, then 100% — letting teams observe error rates and latency before full cutover.

clues.clue: This zero-downtime deployment approach maintains two identical production environments but routes all traffic with a single load-balancer flip, enabling instant rollback by flipping back.
clues.explain: Blue-green keeps two identical production stacks; traffic switches from the live (blue) to the new (green) in one flip, allowing instant rollback if errors appear — no gradual ramp required.

clues.clue: This DevSecOps practice analyzes application dependencies and open-source libraries in the CI pipeline for known CVEs before code is merged, often called SCA.
clues.explain: SCA tools (e.g. Snyk, Dependabot, OWASP Dependency-Check) inventory open-source components and map them to the CVE database, blocking merges when high-severity vulnerabilities are found — complementing container image scanning.

clues.clue: This agentless configuration management tool uses YAML playbooks to configure systems over SSH and is developed by Red Hat.
clues.explain: Ansible is an agentless automation tool that connects to managed hosts over SSH, applies YAML-defined tasks from playbooks, and requires no daemon installed on target nodes.

clues.clue: This reusable Ansible unit packages tasks, handlers, files, and templates together so they can be shared across playbooks and installed via Ansible Galaxy.
clues.explain: An Ansible role is a self-contained, reusable bundle of tasks, handlers, variables, and templates; roles are shared on Ansible Galaxy and included in playbooks with the 'roles:' key.

clues.clue: Running `terraform apply` a second time with no configuration changes produces this reassuring result, demonstrating that the operation is idempotent.
clues.response: What is 'No changes' (0 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy)?
clues.explain: Idempotency means applying the same configuration repeatedly converges to the same state with no further changes; Terraform reports 'No changes. Your infrastructure matches the configuration.' on a clean re-run -- the practical proof of an idempotent apply.

clues.clue: This Terraform feature allows teams to store the state file in a shared location such as an S3 bucket and prevents concurrent modifications using a lock mechanism.
clues.response: What is a remote backend (or Terraform remote state)?
clues.explain: A remote backend (e.g. an S3 bucket with state locking -- via DynamoDB or, in recent Terraform versions, S3-native locking -- or Terraform Cloud) stores terraform.tfstate centrally so teams share one source of truth and avoid conflicting simultaneous applies.

clues.clue: In a GitOps workflow, this type of agent runs inside the cluster and continuously reconciles live infrastructure state against the desired state declared in a Git repository.
clues.response: What is a GitOps operator (or reconciliation controller)?
clues.explain: GitOps operators such as Argo CD and Flux run in-cluster and watch a Git repository; when the repo diverges from live state, the operator automatically applies changes to converge them.
